title: O.1 — Bit flags and bit manipulation via std::bitset

blocks.html: On modern computer architectures, the smallest addressable unit of memory is a byte. Since all objects need to have unique memory addresses, this means objects must be at least one byte in size. For most variable types, this is fine. However, for Boolean values, this is a bit wasteful (pun intended). Boolean types only have two states: true (1), or false (0). This set of states only requires one bit to store. However, if a variable must be at least a byte, and a byte is 8 bits, that means a Boolean is using 1 bit and leaving the other 7 unused.
blocks.preview: On modern computer architectures, the smallest addressable unit of memory is a b

blocks.html: In the majority of cases, this is fine -- we’re usually not so hard-up for memory that we need to care about 7 wasted bits (we’re better off optimizing for understandability and maintainability). However, in some storage-intensive cases, it can be useful to “pack” 8 individual Boolean values into a single byte for storage efficiency purposes.

blocks.html: Doing these things requires that we can manipulate objects at the bit level. Fortunately, C++ gives us tools to do precisely this. Modifying individual bits within an object is called bit manipulation.

blocks.title: Bit flags
blocks.html: Bit flags
Up to this point, we’ve used variables to hold single values:
blocks.preview: Up to this point, we’ve used variables to hold single values:

blocks.code:
int foo { 5 }; // assign foo the value 5 (probably uses 32 bits of storage)
std::cout << foo; // print the value 5
blocks.html:
int foo { 5 }; // assign foo the value 5 (probably uses 32 bits of storage)
std::cout << foo; // print the value 5

However, instead of viewing objects as holding a single value, we can instead treat each bit in the object as an independent Boolean value. When individual bits of an object are used as Boolean values, the bits are called bit flags.

blocks.html:
Nomenclature

A bit holding a 0 value is said to be “false”, “off”, or “not set”.
A bit holding a 1 value is said to be “true”, “on”, or “set”.
When a bit is changed from a 0 to a 1 or a 1 to a 0, we say it has been “flipped” or “inverted”.

blocks.html:
As an aside…

In computing, a flag is a value that signals when some condition exists in a program. With a bit flag, a value of true means the condition exists.

Analogously, in the United States, many mailboxes have small (usually red) physical flags attached to the side. When outgoing mail is waiting to be picked up by the carrier, the flag is raised to signal that there is outgoing mail.

Given a sequence of bits, we typically number the bits from right to left, starting with 0 (not 1). Each number denotes a bit position.

blocks.title: Manipulating bits via std::bitset
blocks.html: Manipulating bits via std::bitset

In lesson 5.3 -- Numeral systems (decimal, binary, hexadecimal, and octal) we already showed how to use a std::bitset to print values in binary. However, this isn’t the only useful thing std::bitset can do.
blocks.preview: In lesson 5.3 -- Numeral systems (decimal, binary, hexadecimal, and octal) we al

blocks.html: std::bitset provides 4 key member functions that are useful for doing bit manipulation:
blocks.preview: std::bitset provides 4 key member functions that are useful for doing bit manipu

blocks.html:
• test() allows us to query whether a bit is a 0 or 1.
  • set() allows us to turn a bit on (this will do nothing if the bit is already on).
  • reset() allows us to turn a bit off (this will do nothing if the bit is already off).
  • flip() allows us to flip a bit value from a 0 to a 1 or vice versa.
blocks.preview: test() allows us to query whether a bit is a 0 or 1.set() allows us to turn a bi

blocks.html: Each of these functions takes the position of the bit we want to operate on as their only argument.
blocks.preview: Each of these functions takes the position of the bit we want to operate on as t

blocks.html: Here’s an example:
blocks.preview: Here’s an example:

blocks.html:
#include <bitset>
#include <iostream>

int main()
{
    std::bitset<8> bits{ 0b0000'0101 }; // we need 8 bits, start with bit pattern 0000 0101
    bits.set(3);   // set bit position 3 to 1 (now we have 0000 1101)
    bits.flip(4);  // flip bit 4 (now we have 0001 1101)
    bits.reset(4); // set bit 4 back to 0 (now we have 0000 1101)

    std::cout << "All the bits: " << bits<< '\n';
    std::cout << "Bit 3 has value: " << bits.test(3) << '\n';
    std::cout << "Bit 4 has value: " << bits.test(4) << '\n';

    return 0;
}
This prints:
blocks.preview: This prints:

blocks.text:
All the bits: 00001101
Bit 3 has value: 1
Bit 4 has value: 0
blocks.html:
All the bits: 00001101
Bit 3 has value: 1
Bit 4 has value: 0

blocks.html: Giving our bits names can help make our code more readable:
blocks.preview: Giving our bits names can help make our code more readable:

blocks.html:
#include <bitset>
#include <iostream>

int main()
{
    [[maybe_unused]] constexpr int  isHungry   { 0 };
    [[maybe_unused]] constexpr int  isSad      { 1 };
    [[maybe_unused]] constexpr int  isMad      { 2 };
    [[maybe_unused]] constexpr int  isHappy    { 3 };
    [[maybe_unused]] constexpr int  isLaughing { 4 };
    [[maybe_unused]] constexpr int  isAsleep   { 5 };
    [[maybe_unused]] constexpr int  isDead     { 6 };
    [[maybe_unused]] constexpr int  isCrying   { 7 };

    std::bitset<8> me{ 0b0000'0101 }; // we need 8 bits, start with bit pattern 0000 0101
    me.set(isHappy);      // set bit position 3 to 1 (now we have 0000 1101)
    me.flip(isLaughing);  // flip bit 4 (now we have 0001 1101)
    me.reset(isLaughing); // set bit 4 back to 0 (now we have 0000 1101)

    std::cout << "All the bits: " << me << '\n';
    std::cout << "I am happy: " << me.test(isHappy) << '\n';
    std::cout << "I am laughing: " << me.test(isLaughing) << '\n';

    return 0;
}

blocks.title: The size of std::bitset
blocks.html: The size of std::bitset

One potential surprise is that std::bitset is optimized for speed, not memory savings. The size of a std::bitset is typically the number of bytes needed to hold the bits, rounded up to the nearest sizeof(size_t), which is 4 bytes on 32-bit machines, and 8-bytes on 64-bit machines.
blocks.preview: One potential surprise is that std::bitset is optimized for speed, not memory sa

blocks.html: Thus, a std::bitset<8> will typically use either 4 or 8 bytes of memory, even though it technically only needs 1 byte to store 8 bits. Thus, std::bitset is most useful when we desire convenience, not memory savings.

blocks.title: Querying std::bitset
blocks.html: Querying std::bitset
There are a few other member functions that are often useful:
blocks.preview: There are a few other member functions that are often useful:

blocks.html:
• size() returns the number of bits in the bitset.
  • count() returns the number of bits in the bitset that are set to true.
  • all() returns a Boolean indicating whether all bits are set to true.
  • any() returns a Boolean indicating whether any bits are set to true.
  • none() returns a Boolean indicating whether no bits are set to true.
blocks.preview: size() returns the number of bits in the bitset.count() returns the number of bi

blocks.html:
#include <bitset>
#include <iostream>

int main()
{
    std::bitset<8> bits{ 0b0000'1101 };
    std::cout << bits.size() << " bits are in the bitset\n";
    std::cout << bits.count() << " bits are set to true\n";

    std::cout << std::boolalpha;
    std::cout << "All bits are true: " << bits.all() << '\n';
    std::cout << "Some bits are true: " << bits.any() << '\n';
    std::cout << "No bits are true: " << bits.none() << '\n';
    
    return 0;
}
This prints:
blocks.preview: This prints:

8 bits are in the bitset
3 bits are set to true
All bits are true: false
Some bits are true: true
No bits are true: false
